speaker: Casey Handmer
title: Why Elon Outcompetes Everyone | Casey Handmer, Terraform Industries
question: In heavy industrial and energy infrastructure, why do major operators invest in building duplicate facilities in competing jurisdictions even when their primary site is already established?
guest: Well, Elon's in the process of undergoing regulatory arbitrage. The impression I get is that the Rio Grande Valley authorities having jurisdiction were perhaps getting a little too comfortable with their monopoly on Starship development and the enormous revenue it brought to that area, and potentially becoming too extractive. So how do you make sure you keep that relationship healthy? You create an escape hatch that has near-zero cost to hold and huge leverage, and then you can run regulatory arbitrage. If push comes to shove, he will do to Texas what he did to California and say, 'I'm taking my business elsewhere,' because you can shear the sheep, but you can't skin them. If you shear the sheep, it makes more wool; if you skin it, it dies. So you don't want to cut too deep.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Major operators build duplicate facilities in rival jurisdictions mainly to reduce dependence on any single government, regulator, or market. A plant, refinery, LNG terminal or pipeline is an immobile, decades-long asset; once it is built, the host state gains leverage and can raise taxes or royalties, tighten permitting, impose export controls, or even expropriate. A credible second site restores the operator's bargaining power, because production can be shifted if terms deteriorate.

Duplication also hedges physical and geopolitical risk: sanctions, war, trade barriers, natural disasters, strikes, or grid and feedstock disruptions at one site do not halt the whole business. It secures market access too, since tariffs, local-content rules and subsidies (such as the US Inflation Reduction Act or European incentives) often reward producing inside the jurisdiction, and it lets firms play governments against each other for incentives.

Finally, there are commercial benefits: proximity to different customers and feedstocks, lower transport costs, currency and energy-price diversification, and assurance to customers and lenders that supply is resilient.

The redundancy costs some efficiency, but it buys optionality and insurance against concentrated risk.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Major industrial and energy operators build duplicate facilities in competing jurisdictions primarily to hedge regulatory, geopolitical, and operational risks while preserving bargaining leverage. Once an operator commits billions in sunk capital to a single site, it faces the classic hold-up problem: host governments, utilities, or labor groups can raise taxes, tighten permitting rules, or hike tariffs knowing an immobile asset cannot easily relocate. Maintaining parallel capacity across borders creates credible production-shifting options that discipline local stakeholders and unlock competing subsidies, tax abatements, and favorable power contracts.

Geographic duplication also delivers essential physical and commercial resilience. Splitting output across independent power grids, transport corridors, and weather zones insulates customers from natural disasters, grid failures, and political disruptions. Furthermore, secondary sites bypass trade barriers, local-content mandates, and physical scaling limits at the primary hub, such as grid interconnection queues or pipeline bottlenecks. Ultimately, sacrificing single-site economies of scale serves as a strategic insurance premium that protects supply continuity and caps exposure to any single jurisdiction.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer: Major operators build duplicate facilities in rival jurisdictions mainly to hedge risk and keep leverage, not because they need more capacity. One site is a single point of failure. A hurricane, earthquake, grid failure, fire or strike can shut it down, and a second plant keeps supply going to customers who expect uninterrupted output. Political and regulatory risk matters just as much. Tax regimes, permitting rules, carbon pricing, export controls and tariffs can change sharply. Being present in several jurisdictions lets a firm move production to wherever conditions are best, and a credible threat to do so gives it bargaining power when it negotiates subsidies, power prices or labor terms. Governments often pay for these second sites. Examples include US Inflation Reduction Act credits, EU state aid and local-content rules that require production inside a market before a firm can sell there or win contracts. Sites near the end customer also cut freight costs, avoid trade barriers and make supply chains more secure, which is valuable at a time when geopolitics is pushing companies toward "friend-shoring." Finally, owning a second site keeps competitors from taking scarce resources such as grid connections, ports, water rights and skilled workers in a fast-growing region.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Major industrial and energy operators build duplicate facilities in competing jurisdictions primarily to manage risk, capture incentives, and preserve bargaining leverage. Relying on a single site exposes capital-intensive operations to localized disruptions such as extreme weather, grid failures, labor disputes, or sudden regulatory shifts; a second jurisdiction provides operational redundancy and supply continuity during outages or maintenance. Just as importantly, geographic duplication mitigates the "hold-up" problem: once heavy infrastructure is sunk in one location, host governments can raise taxes or tighten rules, so maintaining a viable alternative strengthens the operator's negotiating position while letting it capture competing tax credits, subsidies, or cheaper feedstocks. Finally, duplicating capacity closer to distinct regional markets or export corridors lowers transportation costs, circumvents tariffs and local-content rules, and allows operators to expand when their primary site hits physical, environmental, or grid constraints.

A second facility gives an operator something an established site alone cannot provide: a credible alternative. Heavy industrial and energy facilities are expensive to move and often depend on local permits, power prices, taxes, and transport links. Once a company has committed capital to one site, it has less leverage if those terms change. A plant in another jurisdiction lets it shift some production or steer future expansion elsewhere, strengthening its hand in negotiations with governments, utilities, and suppliers.

The second site can also keep customers supplied during outages or disruptions and provide access to cheaper energy, new markets, or local incentives. Operators make the investment when those benefits, including the flexibility to respond to future changes, outweigh the cost of duplicating capacity.

For a major operator, the investment can pay off through fewer interruptions and better terms across its operations, even if the duplicate facility sometimes runs below capacity.
